# 1 What this case study shows

This vignette presents an application case study. It does not present
calibration evidence.

The case study applies the `stablr` environment-stability workflow to a real
aging atlas. The goal is to find cell types whose blood proportions track
age in the same way in every cohort. A second goal is to predict age from
the selected cell types on cohorts that the model never saw.

The analysis ran once with a fixed seed. The full script is
`inst/benchmarks/ws8_aging_showcase.R` in the package source. The figures
here come from that run. The run takes about 15 minutes, so this vignette
shows the saved results instead of recomputing them.

# 2 The data

The data come from a public healthy-aging PBMC atlas of eight scRNA-seq
cohorts (Terekhova et al. 2026, *Immunity*). The cohorts differ in size,
ancestry mix, and age range:

| Cohort | Donors |
|---|---|
| OneK1K | 981 |
| AIDA | 625 |
| CIMA | 421 |
| KCL | 188 |
| ABF300 | 166 |
| UCSF | 99 |
| SoundLife | 96 |
| SPAC | 33 |
| **Total** | **2609** |

Each donor is one sample. The features are 59 cell-type proportions from the
published annotations, add-half smoothed and logit transformed. One covariate
(sex) joins the panel. Three covariate columns (CMV status and two ancestry
indicators) are constant inside at least one cohort, so the analysis drops
them. A column that is constant inside a cohort has no within-cohort signal,
and its zero variance breaks the equicorrelated knockoff construction. The
final panel has 60 features. No cell-type feature is constant in any cohort.

The outcome is donor age in years. The environments are the eight cohorts.

# 3 Method settings

The analysis uses `stabl_environment_stability()` with these settings:

- Base learner: random forest (`ranger`) with model-X equicorrelated knockoff
  artificial features.
- 200 bootstrap resamples per cohort, classic bootstrap design
  (`sample_fraction = 1`, `replace = TRUE`).
- Selection rule: a feature is "consistent" when its minimum
  max-over-lambda stability score across the eight cohorts is at least 0.5
  (the min-agg rule).
- Sensitivity analysis: lasso with the same knockoff type and seed.
- Age prediction: leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO). Each fold trains a ridge
  model on seven cohorts and predicts the eighth.

The random forest learner is calibrated for scoped settings: gaussian
problems with up to a few dozen predictors. This panel has 60 features, close
to that scope. See `?make_ranger_adapter` for the benchmark numbers and the
exact limits.

# 4 Result: features that track age in every cohort

The min-agg rule selects **24 of the 60 features**. Figure 1 ranks all
features by their minimum cross-cohort stability score. The dashed line is
the 0.5 selection bar. Crosses mark the eight features that the source
publication predeclared as age-associated.

![Minimum cross-cohort stability scores](figures/ws8_min_scores.png)

Seven of the eight predeclared features pass the bar:

| Predeclared feature | Min-agg result |
|---|---|
| CD8+ T Naive | selected |
| CD8+ RTE | selected |
| CD4+ RTE | selected |
| MAIT | selected |
| CD4+ Temra | selected |
| CD8+ Temra | selected |
| CD8+ Tem GZMK+ | selected |
| CD8+ Tem GZMB+ | not selected (score 0.45) |

Figure 2 shows why the min-agg rule is strict. Each panel shows the Spearman
correlation between the feature and age, per cohort, for the 24 selected
features. The top features keep the same sign in all eight cohorts. The
naive and RTE compartments fall with age everywhere. MAIT falls with age
everywhere. The bottom rows of the plot show features that pass the bar with
weaker or mixed correlations; the min-agg score still required selection
frequency above 0.5 in every single cohort.

![Per-cohort age correlations of the selected features](figures/ws8_consistency_heatmap.png)

The lasso sensitivity analysis selects 6 features under the same min-agg
rule. CD8+ T Naive is the only feature that both learners select. This
agreement is partial, not full. The lasso result supports the direction of
the primary result; it does not reproduce the full 24-feature panel.

# 5 Result: age prediction on held-out cohorts

The LOCO design asks a hard question: does a model trained on seven cohorts
predict age in the eighth? The mean absolute error (MAE) is 12.1 years for
ridge on all 60 features and 11.7 years for ridge on the 24 selected
features.

| Cohort | n | MAE all features | MAE selected |
|---|---|---|---|
| ABF300 | 166 | 9.30 | 9.43 |
| AIDA | 625 | 14.60 | 14.11 |
| CIMA | 421 | 15.60 | 7.62 |
| KCL | 188 | 9.67 | 10.27 |
| OneK1K | 981 | 15.47 | 17.65 |
| SoundLife | 96 | 6.75 | 9.56 |
| SPAC | 33 | 12.33 | 14.32 |
| UCSF | 99 | 13.41 | 10.83 |

Figure 3 shows predicted versus observed age for the selected-feature model,
one panel per held-out cohort. Predictions track age in every cohort, but
each cohort shows its own compression toward the middle of its age range.
OneK1K predictions cluster between 40 and 60 years. SPAC shows discrete
bands because it has 33 donors and few distinct ages. The source publication
reports 8.2 years test MAE for its trained clock. Our protocol is simpler
and different: a ridge model on donor-level proportions, trained on seven
cohorts and applied to the eighth. The two numbers are not directly
comparable. The honest reading is that composition features alone carry
cross-cohort age signal, with cohort-specific calibration loss.

![LOCO predicted versus observed age](figures/ws8_loco_calibration.png)

# 6 Scope and limits

Three limits matter for reuse.

First, this is an application case study, not a calibration study. The
calibration evidence for the random-forest learner comes from simulation
(`?make_ranger_adapter`). The simulation covers gaussian problems with up to
a few dozen predictors. This panel has 60 features and one strong covariate
structure. The showcase shows the workflow on real data; it does not add
calibration guarantees.

Second, the min-agg rule is conservative by design. A feature must be
selected in every cohort. Features with cohort-specific signal fail the bar
even when their biology is real. The 0.45 score of CD8+ Tem GZMB+ is an
example: it is close to the bar but not above it.

Third, the age-prediction numbers inherit the cohort differences. The
publication itself reports that cohort identity is the largest variance
component in the atlas. The LOCO errors reflect that structure. They are not
a claim about the best achievable age clock.
